titulo: The Left That Carried Out the Adjustment
subtitulo: The Chinese Piraeus, Prespa, and what happens to a party that does the opposite of what it promised (2015 – 2019)

coda.heading: Coda for the trip: what to look for
intro: If your flight or your route brings you near Piraeus, look at it. It is the port from entrega 1 — the one that made the rowers' democracy and the Delian empire possible — now a Chinese container terminal and a ferry station to the islands. Few material continuities of twenty-five hundred years are so literal, and few transfers of ownership so eloquent. If you take a ferry from there, spend twenty minutes watching the cranes.

items.text: In Athens, look for some of the self-organized social structures that survived the crisis: there are solidarity clinics, no-middleman markets, and community centers in Exarchia, Kypseli, and other neighborhoods, many with publicly announced activities. If you can get a half-hour conversation with someone from one of those networks, you will have the best ethnographic material of your trip, and on ground you already know professionally.

sections.heading: Governing against your own program
paragraphs: After accepting the third memorandum in July 2015, Tsipras called early elections for September and won again. The fact deserves attention: an electorate that had voted no in a referendum re-validated, two months later, the very government that had ignored that result. The most plausible reading is not contradiction but calculation: the public understood that no alternative was available and preferred that the adjustment be administered by whoever had at least tried to avoid it. Part of the party split off; the splinter vanished electorally.

Between 2015 and 2019, a left-wing government carried out the harshest of the three programs: new pension cuts, VAT increases, the opening of protected sectors, labor-market reform, very high required primary surpluses, and a privatization schedule the left itself had denounced. It simultaneously introduced some protective measures — the social solidarity income, the extension of health coverage to the uninsured, partial protection of primary residences against foreclosure — and passed social reforms the right would never have made, such as the legal recognition of gender identity in 2017 and civil unions for same-sex couples in 2015.
Greece formally exited the third program on August 20, 2018, with enhanced surveillance to follow. And in the 2019 elections it lost power to New Democracy.

The interesting sociological question is not whether Tsipras betrayed his cause. It is what happens to a political system when the party that embodies the alternative demonstrates that there is none. The Greek answer was a remarkable demobilization: falling turnout, declining protest, and a normalization of politics that some read as maturity and others as resignation. When the left carries out the right's program because there is no other option, what erodes is not a party but the belief that voting decides anything. That is the heaviest political legacy of the decade, and it explains much of what happens afterward across Europe.

sections.heading: Piraeus: geopolitics on a dock
paragraphs: Among the privatizations the program required, none carries the symbolic and strategic weight of the port of Piraeus. The Chinese state shipping company COSCO had operated two container terminals under concession since 2009; in 2016 the Syriza government completed the sale of a majority stake in the Piraeus Port Authority to COSCO, with its holding expanded later on.

The operational results were remarkable: Piraeus went from a port of modest traffic to being among Europe's leading container ports. And the strategic implications were too: Piraeus is the gateway of China's Belt and Road Initiative into the European market, with a rail connection into the Balkans. Greece joined, in 2019, China's cooperation format with the countries of Central and Eastern Europe — from which others would later withdraw — and in 2017 it blocked a European Union statement on human rights in China, an episode read in Brussels for exactly what it was.

A cold-eyed analysis is called for here. A country forced by its European creditors to privatize sold its principal strategic asset to the only buyer with capital and the will to buy, which happened to be a state rival of those same creditors. European conditionality produced Chinese penetration. There was no conspiracy: there was a sequence of rational decisions that none of the parties fully controlled.

The Peruvian resonance is immediate, and among the most useful in this course of study: the Chancay megaport, with COSCO holding a majority stake, inaugurated in November 2024, is exactly the same operation transplanted to the South American Pacific. A deep-water port capable of reordering the continent's trade routes toward Asia, controlled by the same Chinese state company, with the same consequences in terms of real logistical efficiency and geopolitical exposure, and with the same uneasy reaction from Washington. If you want a single image to explain the world of 2026, Piraeus and Chancay are the same image, ten thousand kilometers apart. And in both cases the pertinent question is not whether China is good or bad, but what bargaining power is left to a state that needs the capital and does not control the infrastructure that results.

sections.heading: Prespa: closing a twenty-seven-year dispute
paragraphs: In June 2018, on Lake Prespa, the foreign ministers of Greece and of what was then the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia signed the agreement that fixed the name North Macedonia, with recognition of the Macedonian nationality and language and an explicit renunciation of any territorial claims or of exclusive claims to the ancient heritage, in exchange for the lifting of Greece's veto on that country's accession to NATO and the European Union.

The agreement cost both governments dearly, politically. In Greece there were mass demonstrations in Thessaloniki and Athens, the breakup of the governing coalition, and a portion of the electorate that never forgave it. In North Macedonia the September 2018 referendum drew insufficient turnout, and ratification proceeded through parliament amid difficulty. As we saw in entrega 3, in May 2024 the new Macedonian president omitted the constitutional name from her oath and the friction reopened, though neither side has renounced the agreement.

It is worth recording the achievement, because this course of study has been rather severe with contemporary politics. Prespa is one of the few recent European cases of a negotiated resolution to an entrenched identity dispute, carried out by two governments that knew they would lose votes over it. Politics can indeed close symbolic conflicts; it is simply almost never in its interest to do so. For Peru, with its own identity disputes and its chronically unresolved socio-environmental conflicts, the case is interesting for exactly that reason: what was missing was never the technical formula, but governments willing to pay the cost of applying it.

sections.heading: What was left of society after the adjustment
paragraphs: It is worth taking stock of what the decade left behind, beyond the macroeconomic aggregates.

First, a more unequal and older social structure, with an entire generation — those who were twenty in 2010 — whose working lives began late, badly, and often abroad. Second, a shrunken and demoralized public sector, with salaries cut and no staff replacement for years: when the pandemic arrived in 2020, Greece faced the emergency with a health system that had spent a decade losing doctors and beds. Third, an economy even more concentrated in tourism, shipping, and real estate, that is, more exposed to external shocks than before the crisis. Fourth, a dense network of self-organized social initiatives — solidarity clinics, no-middleman markets, community kitchens, housing networks — that substituted for the state during the worst years and that constitute, for a sociologist, the most interesting object to emerge from the period.

That fourth point deserves emphasis, because it is where the Peruvian mirror works best. The Greek social clinics of 2012–2016, staffed by volunteers for people with no coverage, are functionally equivalent to Peru's comedores populares and vaso de leche programs of the 1980s: collective subsistence responses to the state's withdrawal, sustained mainly by women, that generate real organizational capacity and always run the same double risk — being co-opted by clientelist politics, or hardening into a permanent substitute that lets the state off the hook for its own obligation. In Peru, ollas comunes reappeared en masse during the 2020 pandemic and are still operating in 2026, forty years after the first ones. Emergency solidarity tends to become institutionalized as managed poverty. It is one of the most important things this course of study can leave you to watch for in Greece.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026
paragraphs: New Democracy has governed since 2019, reelected in 2023. The economy is growing above the European average, tourism sets new records year after year, unemployment fell to single digits for the first time in more than a decade, and in 2023 the country recovered its investment grade. In the vocabulary of the markets, Greece is the recovered pupil.

At the same time, real wages remain below pre-crisis levels, housing prices in Athens and on the islands have risen sharply, driven by short-term rentals and by golden-visa residency permits, poverty and material deprivation remain among the highest in the Union, and institutional trust remains in the basement of European rankings. And there are two open fronts that the next entrega and the one after it examine: the migration border, and the Tempi rail disaster, which in 2023 and 2025 brought more people into the streets than any event since the crisis.

The coexistence of a country doing well and a society that does not feel it is the defining feature of the Greece of 2026, and it is exactly the same diagnosis one could make of Peru over the last decade: sustained macroeconomic solidity alongside social, institutional, and expectational decay. In both cases, the gap between the indicators and the experience is the space where disaffection grows, and where whatever comes next is decided.
